tldr: This paper proposes "AAAI," an integrated architecture where autonomous robot AI recognizes the physical aging of its own hardware, adapting inference workloads and planning to extend operational life.
hero_caption: Overall structure of the AAAI framework. The hardware degradation models (Pillar 1), self-adaptive reasoning engine (Pillar 2), and survival-centric intelligence strategy (Pillar 3) work in tandem, transitioning across three operational modes according to the degree of aging to achieve high resilience.
overview:
In autonomous systems operating in environments where maintenance is impossible for long periods—such as deep-sea exploration, space missions, and implantable medical devices—battery degradation, sensor drift, and processor thermal wear are inevitable. However, current AI is designed under the assumption that hardware remains in its mint condition. Consequently, even without a single component completely failing, an accumulation of degradation can lead to "agnostic collapse," where the mission suddenly breaks down one day.

To address this, the authors propose Aging-Aware Autonomous Intelligence (AAAI), a framework in which the machine recognizes its own "aging" in real time and autonomously adjusts the burden of its reasoning and planning. Rather than introducing new hardware, AAAI is a software architecture that integrates material science physics-of-failure models with the cognitive layer of AI into a closed loop.

Specifically, it tracks health scalars across power, sensing, memory, and computation, continuously switching computational algorithms, shortening planning horizons, and concentrating resources on critical functions. Grounded in simulations and existing knowledge, the authors demonstrate that embedding adaptive intelligence that anticipates hardware aging prevents abrupt mission collapse, avoids transitioning into premature safety modes, and maximizes operational lifetime.
contributions: Defining the concept of "agnostic collapse," where an AI suddenly fails due to compound aging rather than a single component fault.
Systematizing "AAAI," a three-pillar architecture that directly connects physics-of-failure-based hardware health estimation to AI inference, planning, and decision-making layers.

Presenting an operational methodology that uses proportional control to scale down inference models and compress planning horizons according to degradation, gradually transitioning from normal operation to graceful degradation.

Structuring the importance of embodied intelligence that recognizes hardware state, along with safety design criteria, for extreme environments such as spacecraft, marine robotics, and implantable medical devices.

sections.heading: Aging Unnoticed Beneath the Sea: The Divide Between AI and Hardware
sections.summary: Using the example of an underwater exploration robot inspecting subsea pipelines for two years, this section points out the severe gap between physical hardware degradation and the assumptions in AI software. It raises the issue that although individual component wear is physically predictable, it is not reflected in operational planning.
sections.details:
Imagine an autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) that has been inspecting a subsea pipeline for two years. Its battery capacity has dropped to a fraction of its original rating, its depth sensor has developed drift (a measurement offset over time), and its processor runs hot under continuous computational thermal loads.

Despite this, the onboard software keeps planning as if the system were brand new, attempting to execute heavy tasks that the aging hardware can no longer reliably handle. A serious disconnect exists in autonomous system design.

Electrochemical degradation of batteries, sensor drift, and the thermal aging of embedded processors are well understood in materials science and reliability engineering. Yet, most AI systems deployed in the field do not integrate real-time hardware health into planning and decision-making. As a result, the mismatch between "assumed capability" and "actual physical capability" snowballs, ultimately surfacing as mission failure.

sections.heading: The Inconvenient Contract AI Silently Signs: "Hardware Stays Brand New"
sections.summary: Modern AI implicitly assumes that sensors, batteries, and memory will always perform to catalog specs, but physical degradation proceeds irreversibly. An engineering approach that binds materials science knowledge into the AI reasoning layer has long been overlooked.
sections.details:
Modern AI systems implicitly assume a stable hardware contract: sensors faithfully measure the outside world, batteries provide rated energy, processors execute without error, and memory accurately retains written data. In the short term, this assumption poses no problem, but in long-term field deployments, it inevitably breaks down.

The physical phenomena of hardware degradation have been scientifically understood for decades.
- Lithium-ion batteries undergo irreversible electrochemical changes with every charge-discharge cycle, forming surface films on electrodes and losing capacity according to Arrhenius kinetics.
- Silicon processors experience a gradual erosion of transistor timing margins due to sustained voltage stress.
- Memory cells accumulate radiation-induced bit flips, with error rates climbing over time and with higher temperatures.
- Spacecraft solar arrays lose approximately 20% to 40% of their output during their first decade of operation due to radiation damage.

These are not exceptional glitches; they are the inevitable physical trajectory of deployed hardware. An AI system that fails to account for this reality inevitably drifts out of alignment with the platform supporting it. While materials scientists have modeled degradation processes in great detail, virtually no framework has asked how an AI should adapt its reasoning as measurable wear advances.

sections.heading: The Anatomy of "Agnostic Collapse": Creeping Degradation, Not Sudden Faults
sections.summary: This section defines "agnostic collapse," where creeping degradation accumulates past a threshold to cause mission failure, rather than a sudden single-component breakdown. Mechanisms are needed to avoid two failure modes: destroying itself by forcing heavy computing, or retiring prematurely out of excessive caution.
sections.details:
The authors term this overlooked mode of failure "agnostic collapse." Rather than a sudden failure like a single component breaking, it occurs when gradual performance drifts—undetected by conventional diagnostic tests—accumulate and fall below required operational margins. The hardware did not break; rather, a hardware-unaware control system simply aged past its operational envelope.

This pattern appears prominently in simulations of autonomous marine vessels. In the early stages of a mission, task performance remains high, but as normal wear like reduced battery capacity and declining sensor accuracy progresses, control performance suddenly drops. Two typical failure modes emerge here:
- First, the system continues heavy tasks like deep learning inference, long-horizon planning, and high-resolution sensing despite hardware decline, exceeding physical limits and collapsing.
- Second, the system over-detects anomalies and retreats prematurely into a conservative safe mode, needlessly abandoning usable remaining capacity.

While existing prognostics techniques can predict component lifetimes, they do not tell an AI how to change its reasoning or planning within its remaining life. Hardware redundancy also hits its limits in resource-constrained compact platforms. What is needed is a cognitive response that adapts thought processes to an aging body.

sections.heading: Current State of the Art: Halting at Monitoring Without Reaching "Thought"
sections.summary: This section reviews four existing domains: physics-of-failure models, autonomous lifecycle management, proactive lifetime extension, and cross-layer co-design. All remain limited to resource allocation or static optimization, missing the cognitive integration that adapts reasoning and planning to hardware states during runtime.
sections.details:
In recent years, AI-based equipment health monitoring has progressed, but most of it remains confined to the hardware management layer (wear detection and local protection). It does not reach "cognitive adaptation," where an agent actively reasons about its physical state to modify plans and priorities. The authors categorize prior work into four pillars and clarify their limitations.

### Pillar 1: Hardware Self-Awareness
Physics-of-failure models have established a solid theoretical foundation. Methods like detecting time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB) or tracking negative-bias temperature instability (NBTI) for real-time transistor aging are practical. However, these signals are only used for engineer alerts or local register adjustments; they never alter what the system pursues or how it reasons.

### Pillar 2: Autonomous Lifecycle Management
Algorithms exist to balance active and standby components autonomously, reconciling performance and longevity. However, this remains an optimization at the resource allocation layer, without direct ties to high-level mission planning.

### Pillar 3: Proactive Lifetime Extension
Approaches like ReaLM exploit the numerical tolerance of neural networks to lower power consumption while preserving performance, alongside circuit-level aging-adaptive voltage scaling. Yet, these techniques operate in isolation within their respective layers.

### Pillar 4: Cross-Layer Co-Design
Methods such as HAWQ-V2 assign bitwidths based on quantization vulnerability or route tasks to less-degraded, reliable chip regions. However, these fix the software-hardware relationship at build/design time and do not provide the ability to flexibly adapt reasoning as the body ages during runtime.

sections.heading: Bridging the Divide: The Leap from Monitoring to Real-Time Decision-Making
sections.summary: What existing approaches lack is cognitive integration: uniting health metrics from multiple subsystems in real time and coupling them directly with mission strategy. AAAI's novelty lies in assembling these existing component technologies into a closed-loop cognitive architecture.
sections.details:
Existing research has addressed hardware health monitoring and model complexity matching in isolation, but they have never been unified into a cognitive function. Specifically, no prior comprehensive architecture continuously estimates health across multiple subsystems—power, sensing, memory, and computation—to dynamically shape reasoning, planning, and mission strategy in real time.

The core contribution of AAAI is not the invention of novel specialized hardware. Instead, it lies in an architectural design that organically connects fragmented components across materials science, reliability engineering, embedded control, and AI algorithms into a closed-loop cognitive system.

sections.heading: The First Pillar to Age Gracefully: Quantifying "One's Own Aging" with Physics Models
sections.summary: The first pillar of AAAI tracks the health of power, sensing, memory, and computation in real time as scalar values in $[0, 1]$. Rather than monitoring single components in isolation, its strength lies in capturing compound, correlated degradation accelerated simultaneously by factors like temperature or salt exposure.
sections.details:
The first pillar of Aging-Aware Autonomous Intelligence (AAAI) is true hardware self-awareness. It represents the state of four critical subsystems—power, sensing, memory, and computation—as continuous health scalars $h \in [0, 1]$, where $1$ denotes pristine condition and $0$ indicates failure, updating them in real time using physics-of-failure models.

Crucially, degradation across subsystems does not proceed independently. Severe environmental stress damages multiple components simultaneously.
- For instance, high-temperature environments accelerate battery wear while significantly degrading processor operational reliability.
- Salt exposure in marine environments triggers sensor corrosion alongside degradation in surrounding circuitry.

AAAI models these correlated degradation dynamics as interconnected processes rather than isolated components. This allows the system to detect early signs of latent collapse spreading across the platform long before individual components reach critical thresholds.

captions.F1: AAAI system architecture diagram. Degradation data from hardware (power, sensing, memory, computation) at the top is aggregated by the cognitive aging model (Pillar 1), flowing through the reasoning engine (Pillar 2) and survival strategy (Pillar 3) to be reflected in three operational modes.

sections.heading: The Second Pillar of Thinking Within Limits: Dynamically Scaling Reasoning and Planning
sections.summary: The second pillar, the self-adaptive reasoning engine, continuously modulates AI model complexity, planning horizons, and task queue priorities according to health levels. Proportional control matched to residual capability prevents task collapse without relying on jarring discrete mode shifts.
sections.details:
Hardware self-awareness is meaningless unless it reflects in actual behavior. The second pillar of AAAI is the self-adaptive reasoning engine, which dynamically modulates task scope and complexity based on available hardware capacity.

When computational resources and memory are healthy, the system deploys large deep learning models and adopts long planning horizons to find optimal actions. However, once hardware capacity decline is detected, the system adapts proportionally:
- Switching inference models to lightweight alternative architectures
- Shortening planning horizons to reduce computational burden
- Reordering the task queue to prioritize tasks with the highest utility-to-computation cost ratio

This adaptation is implemented not as jarring, discrete mode shifts, but as continuous, proportional control tracking the hardware's shrinking physical envelope in real time. In boundary zones where conventional hardware-unaware AI would collapse from computational overload, AAAI aligns physical capability with computational load, ensuring mission continuity.

sections.heading: The Third Pillar of Surviving with Purpose: Phased Functional Downscaling and Life-Extension Strategies
sections.summary: The third pillar is a survival strategy that treats operational lifetime itself as an allocatable resource to be optimized. Across three phases—normal operation, resource conservation, and a "graceful withdrawal" preserving only core functions while cutting communications—it continues delivering valuable results until the final moment.
sections.details:
The third pillar, survival-centric intelligence, reframes hardware operating life from a passive consequence into an active resource to be explicitly allocated across competing mission objectives. Its purpose is to maximize overall mission utility within a finite lifespan.

This strategy is realized through three adaptive operational modes:
- **Full health**: Normal operation with all functions fully active.
- **Conservation zone**: Once signs of wear emerge, the system transitions to protect mission-critical functions while curbing resource consumption.
- **Minimal core / Graceful withdrawal**: In the final stage, non-essential subsystems are shut down according to pre-computed priorities. Actions are restricted to a minimal operational core, and communication frequency is drastically cut to extend operational life to the absolute limit.

This is not a catastrophic crash, but a planned "graceful degradation." The system continues performing scientifically valuable sensing and secure data preservation until its very last breath.

sections.heading: Practices in Space, Deep-Sea, and Medicine—and New Risks Borne by Autonomous Intelligence
sections.summary: This section explains utility in extreme environments like LEO satellites, marine robots, and pacemakers. It also addresses risks like "mode confusion" arising from AI autonomously changing operational modes, arguing for the necessity of safety architectures guaranteeing human intervention.
sections.details:
In practical terms, this architecture offers tremendous benefits in unserviceable, extreme environments.
- **Low Earth Orbit (LEO) microsatellites**: Subjected to constant thermal cycling and ionizing radiation, processors and memory degrade. Applying AAAI allows the system to throttle processor workloads during high thermal stress orbital phases, significantly extending mission lifetime.
- **Marine and offshore robotics**: In environments marked by hydrostatic pressure, vibration, and corrosion, the system actively sheds load to protect essential functions before catastrophic failure occurs.
- **Implantable pacemakers**: Unexpected component aging causing premature battery depletion means revision surgery. Forecasting life to optimize power consumption directly protects patient lives.

What these share is abandoning the assumption that performance stays constant until failure. Without developing new exotic materials or processors, these benefits are achieved simply by having AI act based on physical degradation forecasts.

At the same time, the authors issue a clear warning about new risks. An AI that self-estimates hardware state and autonomously changes decisions risks making operational choices unanticipated or unapproved by human designers. As seen in aviation mode-confusion accidents, small perceptual drifts can lead to catastrophic failures. Therefore, transitions like moving into minimal core mode must be governed by transparent, explicit rules, anchored by strict safety architectures featuring fail-safe provisions and human-in-the-loop oversight.

sections.heading: Toward Embodied Intelligence: Next-Generation Autonomous Systems Facing Physical Constraints
sections.summary: The paper concludes that AI should be reframed not as pure software severed from its computing substrate, but as "embodied intelligence" inseparable from physical aging. It calls for interdisciplinary collaboration to overcome challenges like failure model accuracy and computational overhead.
sections.details:
As autonomous systems venture into harsh environments where maintenance and replacement are impossible, the traditional assumption that AI computation can be abstracted away from physical hardware no longer holds. Hardware degradation is not an anomalous glitch; it is a physical reality proceeding continuously according to the laws of electrochemistry, thermal stress, and radiation damage.

AAAI introduces a paradigm shift: redefining AI not as an unconstrained abstract algorithm, but as embodied intelligence that accepts and responds to irreversible physical aging. By monitoring component health, capturing correlated degradation across subsystems, and adapting behavior to physical limits, it extends operational life and prevents sudden mission collapse.

Of course, challenges remain:
- The accuracy of physics-of-failure models fluctuates with real-world operating conditions.
- Pre-modeling complex, cascading compound degradation is difficult.
- The computational overhead of continuous health monitoring itself can impose a new burden on aging hardware.

Solving these challenges demands interdisciplinary collaboration across materials science, reliability engineering, control theory, embedded systems, and artificial intelligence—a challenge the authors conclude is decisive for establishing next-generation autonomous technology.

takeaways: The importance of not treating hardware specifications as static values in AI design, but embedding degradation-aware physical models into the inference loop.

The effectiveness of proportional control that continuously scales down computational complexity and planning horizons, rather than a binary choice between running or shutting down via fault diagnostics.
The perspective of focusing on correlated degradation across multiple subsystems tied together by thermal and environmental factors, rather than monitoring components in isolation.
The necessity of building self-adaptive AI alongside strict constraint standards and safety architectures to prevent unintended mode transitions.
limitations: Physics-of-failure model estimation accuracy depends heavily on complex, real-world operational environments.
The difficulty of comprehensively pre-modeling cascading compound degradation across multiple intertwined subsystems in harsh conditions.
The computational overhead of continuously monitoring and estimating hardware health in real time, which adds burden to an already aging processor.
The paper focuses primarily on conceptual design and framework formulation, leaving a need for extensive, long-term empirical validation data on physical hardware.
